source: NCERT Class XII, Themes in Indian History, Theme 1. Dating follows this NCERT reprint (total span 6000–1300 BCE).

sections.heading: 1. Basics, Terminology & Chronology
points: **Also known as:** Indus Valley Civilisation. The name "Harappa" derives from the place where the civilisation was first identified.
**Most distinctive artefact:** the seal — usually made of steatite, bearing animal motifs and an undeciphered script.
**Total span (this reprint):** 6000 BCE – 1300 BCE.

sub: Early Harappan — 6000–2600 BCE (formative phase)
Mature Harappan — 2600–1900 BCE (urban, most prosperous phase)
Late Harappan — 1900–1300 BCE (decadent/decline phase)

points: Emergence from early farming communities dated c. 7000 BCE; the urban phase was a result of gradual internal development, not sudden.
**Extent** — Pakistan: Afghanistan, Baluchistan, Sind, Punjab. India: Jammu & Kashmir, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharashtra.
**Sites:** more than 2000 discovered; most between the Indus and Saraswati basins; ~two-thirds in the Saraswati basin.
**Five major cities:** Rakhigarhi, Mohenjodaro, Harappa, Dholavira, Ganweriwala. (Others = regional centres, agricultural villages, ports, manufacturing centres.)
**Site sizes:** Rakhigarhi (biggest, ~550 ha, Hisar, Haryana) > Mohenjodaro (125 ha) > Chanhudaro (<7 ha).
**Abbreviations:** BP = Before Present; BCE = Before Common Era; CE = Common Era; c. = circa (approximate).

sections.heading: 2. Subsistence Strategies
points: **Grains:** wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea, sesame. Millets → Gujarat sites. Rice finds relatively rare.
**Animals (domesticated):** cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo, pig. Wild: boar, deer, gharial; also fish and fowl. (Unclear whether Harappans hunted or got meat from hunting communities.)
**Specialists:** archaeo-botanists (ancient plants), archaeo-zoologists / zoo-archaeologists (animal bones).

sections.heading: 3. Agricultural Technologies
points: **Ploughing:** inferred from bull representations on seals/terracotta → oxen used. Terracotta plough models at Cholistan and Banawali (Haryana).
**Ploughed field at Kalibangan** (Rajasthan) — Early Harappan level; two sets of furrows at right angles → two crops grown together.
**Harvesting tools:** open question — stone blades in wooden handles vs metal tools.
**Irrigation:** semi-arid lands; canals traced at Shortughai (Afghanistan) but not in Punjab/Sind; likely well-water; reservoirs at Dholavira (Gujarat).

sections.heading: 4. Mohenjodaro — Planned Urban Centre (Town Planning)
points: Harappa discovered first, but damaged by brick robbers; Cunningham (1875) noted bricks enough for ~100 miles of railway (Lahore–Multan). Mohenjodaro far better preserved.
**Two divisions:** Citadel (smaller, higher, on mud-brick platforms, walled) + Lower Town (larger, lower, also walled).
**Labour scale:** ~four million person-days estimated just for foundation platforms.
**Bricks:** standardised ratio 4:2:1 (length:breadth:height), sun-dried or baked, uniform across ALL settlements → sign of planning/authority.

sub: Streets on a grid pattern, intersecting at right angles.
Streets & drains laid first, houses built along them; every house had ≥1 wall on a street.
House drains → sump/cesspit (solids settle, waste water flows to street drains).
Main channels: bricks in mortar, covered with loose bricks (removable for cleaning); sometimes limestone covers.
Mackay: "the most complete ancient system yet discovered."
Lothal: houses of mud bricks, drains of burnt bricks.

points: **Domestic architecture:** courtyard-centred; privacy (no ground-level windows; entrance hides interior); every house had a brick-paved bathroom; staircases to upper storeys; ~700 wells in Mohenjodaro.

sub: Warehouse — massive, lower brick portions survive (wooden upper decayed).

Great Bath — rectangular tank in a courtyard with corridor on all four sides; two flights of steps (north & south); made watertight with bricks on edge + gypsum mortar; rooms on three sides (one with a large well); water flowed into a huge drain. Nearby: a smaller building with eight bathrooms (four on each side of a corridor). Likely a special ritual bath.

points: **Fortification variations:** at Dholavira & Lothal the entire settlement was fortified; Lothal's citadel not walled off but built at a height.

sections.heading: 5. Tracking Social Differences
points: **Burials:** dead laid in pits, sometimes brick-lined; some graves had pottery/ornaments (belief in afterlife). Jewellery in burials of both men and women.
**Harappa cemetery** (mid-1980s): ornament of three shell rings + a jasper bead + hundreds of micro beads near skull of a male.
Some had copper mirrors. Overall: Harappans did NOT bury precious things with the dead (contrast with Egyptian pyramids = royal burials with wealth, some contemporaneous).

sub: Utilitarian — daily-use, ordinary material (stone/clay): querns, pottery, needles, flesh-rubbers; found throughout settlements.

Luxuries — rare / costly non-local material / complex technology: e.g. faience (ground sand or silica + colour + gum, fired) miniature pots (possible perfume bottles), concentrated at Mohenjodaro & Harappa, none at small sites like Kalibangan.
Ambiguity: spindle whorls of faience blur the line.

points: **Gold** rare/precious → all gold jewellery recovered from hoards (carefully kept objects, often in pots, never retrieved).

sections.heading: 6. Craft Production
points: **Chanhudaro** (<7 ha): almost exclusively crafts — bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-making, weight-making.
**Bead materials:** carnelian, jasper, crystal, quartz, steatite; copper, bronze, gold; shell, faience, terracotta.
**Bead shapes:** disc, cylindrical, spherical, barrel-shaped, segmented; decorated by incising/painting/etching.
**Techniques:** carnelian red colour by firing yellowish raw material; steatite (soft) moulded from paste → varied shapes; steatite micro bead manufacture = a puzzle.
**Specialised drills:** Chanhudaro, Lothal, Dholavira.
**Coastal shell-working centres:** Nageshwar & Balakot (bangles, ladles, inlay).
**Identifying craft centres:** raw material (stone nodules, whole shells, copper ore), tools, unfinished objects, rejects/waste (waste = best indicator).
Craft production also happened in large cities (Mohenjodaro, Harappa), not only specialised centres.

sections.heading: 7. Procuring Materials & Trade
points: **Local:** clay. Procured from outside the alluvial plain: stone, timber, metal.
**Transport:** terracotta bullock-cart models → land routes; riverine (Indus + tributaries) and coastal routes.

**Strategy 1 — settlements near resources:** Nageshwar/Balakot (shell); Shortughai, Afghanistan (near lapis lazuli — a valued blue stone); Lothal (near carnelian from Bharuch, steatite from south Rajasthan/north Gujarat, metal from Rajasthan).
**Strategy 2 — expeditions:** Khetri, Rajasthan (copper); South India (gold). Steatite micro beads found in these areas = evidence of contact.
**Ganeshwar–Jodhpura culture** (Khetri area): non-Harappan pottery + wealth of copper objects → possibly supplied copper to Harappans.

sub: Oman copper — Omani + Harappan copper both have nickel traces (common origin). A large Harappan jar coated with black clay (prevents liquid percolation) found at Omani sites.
Mesopotamian names: Dilmun = Bahrain, Magan = Oman, Meluhha = Harappan region.
Meluhha products: carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold, wood. Meluhha called a land of seafarers; haja-bird (myth) possibly the peacock.

Seals: a cylinder seal (Mesopotamian type) with humped-bull motif from the Indus; "Persian Gulf" seal in Bahrain with Harappan motifs; Dilmun weights followed the Harappan standard; boat/ship depictions on seals.

sections.heading: 8. Seals, Script & Weights
points: **Seals & sealings:** for long-distance communication; wet clay on a bag's knot, sealed → confirmed non-tampering + sender's identity.

sub: Usually a line of writing (probably name/title of owner); motif conveyed meaning to the illiterate.
Undeciphered; NOT alphabetic (too many signs — 375 to 400).
Most inscriptions short; longest ~26 signs.
Written right to left (wider spacing on right, cramping on left).
Writing found on: seals, copper tools, jar rims, copper/terracotta tablets, jewellery, bone rods, even a signboard (Dholavira).

points: **Weights:** made of chert, generally cubical, no markings. Lower denominations binary (1,2,4,8,16,32); higher decimal (160,200,320,640). Small weights for jewellery/beads. Metal scale-pans found.

sections.heading: 9. Ancient Authority (Polity)
points: **Uniformity of artefacts** (pottery, seals, weights, bricks — uniform ratio from Jammu to Gujarat) → complex, coordinated decisions.
Labour mobilised for bricks, walls, platforms; settlements placed strategically.
**No clear centre of power:** a "palace" at Mohenjodaro (no spectacular finds); "priest-king" stone statue (label borrowed from Mesopotamia; no proof of political power).

sub: No rulers — everybody equal.
Several rulers (Mohenjodaro one, Harappa another…).
A single state (given artefact similarity, planned settlements, standardised bricks, resource-linked settlements) — considered most plausible.

sections.heading: 10. The End of the Civilisation
points: By c. 1800 BCE most Mature Harappan sites (e.g. Cholistan) abandoned; population expanded into Gujarat, Haryana, western UP.

**Post-1900 BCE transformation:** disappearance of weights, seals, special beads; loss of writing, long-distance trade, craft specialisation; deteriorated house-building; no large public structures → rural "Late Harappan" / "successor cultures."
**Explanations:** climatic change, deforestation, excessive floods, shifting/drying of rivers, overuse of landscape — none alone explains the total collapse.

Likely end of a strong unifying element (the Harappan state) — shown by disappearance of seals, script, distinctive beads/pottery; shift from standardised to local weights; abandonment of cities. Subcontinent waited >1000 years for new cities (Ganga valley).

sections.heading: 11. Historiography — Discovering the Civilisation
points: **Cunningham** (first DG, ASI; "father of Indian archaeology"): mid-19th c.; focused on Early Historic (c. 6th BCE–4th CE); used texts + accounts of Chinese Buddhist pilgrims; missed Harappa's significance (believed Indian history began with Ganga-valley cities).
**Daya Ram Sahni** — seals at Harappa; **Rakhal Das Banerji** — similar seals at Mohenjodaro → single culture.

**John Marshall** — announced discovery to the world in 1924; first professional archaeologist in India (experience from Greece/Crete); interested in everyday life too. Flaw: dug uniform horizontal units, ignored stratigraphy → lost context. ("Marshall left India three thousand years older than he had found her" — S.N. Roy.)
**R.E.M. Wheeler** (took over ASI 1944; ex-army brigadier, "military precision"): insisted on following stratigraphy of the mound.

**Post-1947:** major sites went to Pakistan → spurred Indian work (Kutch survey, Punjab, Haryana; excavation of Kalibangan, Lothal, Rakhi Garhi, Dholavira). Since 1980s: international, scientific (surface exploration, minute analysis).

**Stratigraphy concepts:** mound = build-up of occupational debris; layers differ in colour/texture/artefacts; sterile layers = absence of traces (abandonment); lowest = oldest; gives cultural sequence.

sections.heading: 12. Problems of Interpretation (esp. Religion)
points: Material evidence (not the script) reconstructs Harappan life; organic materials decompose, so stone, terracotta, metal survive. Intact valuables are accidental (lost/hoarded), not typical.

**Classifying finds:** by material, and (harder) by function — aided by present-day analogies + context (house/drain/grave/kiln). Clothing known via indirect evidence (sculpture; cotton traces exist).

sub: Heavily jewelled terracotta female figurines → mother goddesses.
Seated one-hand-on-knee male statue → "priest-king."
Great Bath + fire altars (Kalibangan, Lothal) → ritual significance.
Seals with plant motifs → nature worship; one-horned "unicorn" → mythical composite creature.

Cross-legged "yogic" figure surrounded by animals → "proto-Shiva." But the earliest text, the Rigveda (c. 1500–1000 BCE), mentions Rudra (later = Shiva) who is neither Pashupati nor a yogi → mismatch; possibly a shaman.
Conical stones → lingas (a linga = polished stone worshipped as symbol of Shiva) — but could equally be gamesmen (Mackay).

sections.heading: 13. The "Invasion" Debate & Archaeogenetics
points: **Marshall (1931):** "Deadman Lane" skeletons at Mohenjodaro.
**Wheeler (1947):** correlated with Rigveda — pur = fort/rampart; Indra = puramdara (fort-destroyer) → "Indra stands accused" of destroying Harappan cities.

**George Dales (1964, "The Mythical Massacre at Mohenjodaro"):** debunked it — skeletons not of the same period; no destruction level, no burning, no armoured warriors; citadel showed no final defence.

**Rakhigarhi archaeogenetics** (Deccan College Pune + CCMB Hyderabad + Harvard Medical College; Vasant Shinde et al., Cell, 2019): Harappans indigenous; genetic roots to c. 10,000 BCE; lacks steppe-pastoralist / Iranian-farmer ancestry; unbroken continuity ~5000 years; 3D facial reconstructions resemble modern Haryana population.
**Takeaway:** careful re-examination of data can reverse earlier interpretations.

sections.heading: 14. Key Dates — Timeline of Harappan Archaeology

rows: Cunningham's report on a Harappan seal
Daya Ram Sahni — excavations at Harappa
Marshall announces the civilisation to the world

points: **Early Indian archaeology periods** (earliest-evidence dates): Lower Palaeolithic (2 million BP) → Middle (80,000) → Upper (35,000) → Mesolithic (12,000) → Neolithic (10,000) → Chalcolithic (6,000) → Harappan civilisation (2600 BCE) → Early iron/megalithic (1000 BCE) → Early Historic (600 BCE–400 CE).

sections.heading: 15. High-Yield One-Liners (Last-Minute Recall)
points: Seal material = steatite; script = undeciphered, 375–400 signs, right-to-left, longest ~26 signs.
Brick ratio = 4:2:1, uniform everywhere → central authority.
Great Bath steps = N & S; mortar = gypsum.
Weights = chert, cubical; binary low / decimal high.
Wells in Mohenjodaro ≈ 700.
Dilmun = Bahrain, Magan = Oman, Meluhha = Harappan region.
Lapis lazuli → Shortughai (Afghanistan); carnelian → Bharuch; copper → Khetri; gold → South India.
Ploughed field → Kalibangan; reservoirs → Dholavira; shell-work → Nageshwar/Balakot; craft hub → Chanhudaro.
Fire altars → Kalibangan & Lothal.
"Father of Indian archaeology" = Cunningham; announced 1924 = Marshall; stratigraphy/military precision = Wheeler.
Massacre debunked by = George Dales; genome study = Vasant Shinde (2019), Rakhigarhi → indigenous, no steppe/Iranian ancestry.
Biggest Harappan city = Rakhigarhi (~550 ha).

sections.heading: 16. Common UPSC Traps (Watch Out)
points: Great Bath steps are **north & south, NOT east–west**.
Harappan script is **NOT alphabetic** (too many signs).
Rudra in the Rigveda is neither Pashupati nor a yogi (so "proto-Shiva" is a mismatch/speculation).
**Maharashtra IS** in the extent list; **Bihar is NOT**.
Lothal: houses = mud brick, drains = burnt brick.
**Ganweriwala** (not Lothal) is the fifth major city.
The famous ornament at Harappa cemetery was near a **male** skull.
Gold was found only in hoards; Harappans generally did not bury valuables with the dead.
